# Tidy Data and Best Practices in the Use of Spreadsheets

Almost everyone has used a spreadsheet before, and almost everyone has
picked up a few habits along the way that quietly work against them once
that spreadsheet needs to feed into an analysis. This chapter isn't about
learning spreadsheet software — it's about learning to *see* your data the
way a computer does, so that the files you build by hand today don't
become a headache when you (or someone else) tries to read them into R six
months from now.

## What spreadsheets are for (and what they aren't)

Spreadsheets are excellent for one thing in particular: entering data.
They're less well suited to *analyzing* it. It's tempting to sort, filter,
calculate, and summarize directly inside Excel or Google Sheets, since the
tools are right there — but every one of those actions is a manual,
point-and-click step, which means it isn't recorded anywhere and can't be
automatically repeated. If you need to redo the analysis, add new data, or
just remember what you did months later while writing up your methods,
a spreadsheet-based workflow leaves you with no trail to follow. For this
course (and generally, in reproducible research), spreadsheets are a tool
for data entry only — everything downstream of that happens in code.

## Human-readable vs. computer-readable data

Almost every bad spreadsheet habit traces back to the same root cause:
formatting data so that a person can make sense of it, without stopping to
ask whether a computer could too. People are good at picking up meaning
from context — indentation, blank rows, color, a note in the margin. Code
isn't. A script reading in your spreadsheet only sees rows and columns; it
has no way to infer what a blank space or a highlighted cell is supposed
to mean. Getting into the habit of asking "would this still make sense if
all the formatting were stripped away, leaving just the values in a grid?"
is the single most useful check you can run on your own data before
calling it done.

## What makes data "tidy"

The rule at the center of all of this is simple to state: **each column
holds one variable, and each row holds one observation.** A variable is
whatever you're measuring — height, treatment, site, date. An observation
is one instance of measuring all of those things together, for one
subject, at one point in time. When your table is built this way, there's
no ambiguity about what a given column or row represents, either for you
or for the software reading it in. It also happens to line up naturally
with how R (and most statistical languages) actually stores data — as a
set of columns, where every value in a given column has to be the same
type. Once your spreadsheet already matches that structure, importing and
working with it in R takes far less cleanup.

**Try it now:** Look at the most recent spreadsheet you opened in Microsoft 
Excel. For each column, ask yourself: does this column represent
exactly one variable? And for each row: does it represent exactly one
observation? Note down anything that doesn't clearly pass that test — you
don't need to fix it yet, just notice it.

## Common ways spreadsheets go wrong

The tidy data rule is easy to state but easy to violate without realizing
it. Below, we'll walk through the most common patterns to watch for. As
we go, you'll fix a single messy example spreadsheet one problem at a
time, ending with a fully tidy version by the end of the chapter.

Here's the example you'll be working with — a field data sheet recording
frog measurements:

| Site A - collected by M. Brown |         |          |
|---------------------------------|---------|----------|
| Frog ID | Class          | Weight  |
| 1       | adult female   | 12.5g   |
| 2       | juvenile male  |         |
| 3       | Adult Female   | 0       |

[Download the starter spreadsheet](data/frog-data-try-it-now.xlsx) and
open it in Excel or Google Sheets before continuing — you'll build on it
at each checkpoint below.

### Missing data: zero, blank, or something else?

Before we get into specific bad habits, it's worth pausing on one
distinction that trips people up constantly: **a zero and a missing value
are not the same thing.** A zero means you measured something and the
answer was zero — a trap that caught no animals, a plot with no invasive
species present. A missing value means you don't have a number at all —
you didn't get to that measurement, the equipment failed, the observation
wasn't applicable. These are two different facts about your data, and
they need to be recorded differently.

So how *should* you record "missing"? A few options exist, and they're
not equally good:

- **Leaving the cell blank** is generally the best choice. Every common
  analysis tool (including R) recognizes an empty cell as missing data
  and handles it accordingly, without you needing to do anything special.
- **Placeholder numbers** like `999` or `-999` are a common instinct, but
  a computer has no way to know these aren't real measurements — they'll
  silently get pulled into averages and other calculations unless you
  remember to filter them out every single time.
- **Placeholder text** like "Unknown" or "N/A" causes a different problem:
  dropping even one text value into an otherwise numeric column forces
  the *entire column* to be read as text, meaning none of the numbers in
  it can be used in a calculation until that's fixed.
- **Zero** should never be used to mean "missing," for the reason above —
  it erases the distinction between "measured and it was zero" and "not
  measured at all."

The one tradeoff with leaving cells blank: while you're actively entering
data, it can be hard to tell "blank because missing" apart from "blank
because I haven't typed it in yet." Being deliberate and finishing each
row as you go (rather than leaving gaps to fill in "later") helps avoid
that ambiguity.

With that distinction in mind, the frog table above
already reflects it: frog 2's weight is left blank because the scale's
battery died before it could be weighed (truly missing), while frog 3's
weight starts out incorrectly as `0` even though the frog actually
escaped before being weighed — a mistake you'll fix once we get there.

### Cramming two variables into one column

If a single column mixes two pieces of information — say, "adult female"
or "juvenile male" in one "class" column — you've actually got two
variables (age class and sex) squeezed into one. This feels efficient
while entering data, but it backfires the moment you need to filter or
group by just one of those two things: now you have to split the column
apart before you can use it. It's much easier to build the table correctly
from the start than to un-mix a column later, so age class and sex should
each get their own column from the outset.

**Try it now:** Split the "Class" column into two separate columns: "Age
Class" and "Sex." Your table should now look like this:

| Site A - collected by M. Brown |            |        |         |
|---------------------------------|------------|--------|---------|
| Frog ID | Age Class | Sex    | Weight  |
| 1       | adult     | female | 12.5g   |
| 2       | juvenile  | male   |         |
| 3       | Adult     | Female | 0       |

### Putting variables in rows instead of columns

It might seem arbitrary whether variables go in columns and observations
go in rows, rather than the reverse — but there's a concrete reason for
the convention. R stores each column as a vector, and a vector can only
hold one data type at a time (all numbers, or all text, never a mix).
Picture a dataset of frog weights collected from several ponds: if each
frog is a row, you naturally get a numeric "weight" column and a
text "pond" column, which R handles cleanly. Flip that around — with each
frog as a column — and each column ends up holding both a number and a
piece of text, which R can't represent as a single vector at all. This
isn't unique to R; it holds for essentially any tool built around
column-based data.

### Stacking multiple tables in one sheet

Placing more than one table in the same spreadsheet — separated visually
by a blank row, a border, or just physical distance — reads fine to a
person, but a computer parsing that sheet doesn't see separate tables; it
sees rows and columns, and by default will assume any two values on the
same row belong to the same observation. That false association is often
invisible until an analysis produces something obviously wrong, at which
point you're left tracing the error back to a layout choice. If you have
more than one table's worth of information, give each one its own sheet
or its own file. The same idea applies to any note or label sitting
*outside* the table's row-and-column grid — like the "Site A / collected
by M. Brown" note above your frog table — since a computer reading in
just the grid will never see it at all.

**Try it now:** Move the "Site A" and "M. Brown" information out of the
header note and into two proper columns, "Site" and "Observer," repeated
on every row. Your table should now look like this:

| Frog ID | Age Class | Sex    | Weight  | Site   | Observer |
|---------|-----------|--------|---------|--------|----------|
| 1       | adult     | female | 12.5g   | Site A | M. Brown |
| 2       | juvenile  | male   |         | Site A | M. Brown |
| 3       | Adult     | Female | 0       | Site A | M. Brown |

### Splitting data across multiple sheets

This one seems harmless, but it introduces two separate problems. First,
plenty of tools (including base R) can only read one sheet's worth of
data at a time, so working across several tabs means constantly exporting
and re-importing. Second, and more importantly, if you're using separate
sheets to hold the *same kind* of data — say, one tab per field season or
one tab per site — you're violating a closely related tidy data
principle: **each type of observation belongs in one table.** There's no
need to split identical data across sheets; instead, add a column (like
"year" or "site," which you just added above) to record which season or
site each row came from, and keep everything in a single table. That one
change saves you from ever having to stitch sheets back together before
you can analyze anything.

### Using color, borders, or merged cells to encode meaning

Any visual formatting — a highlighted cell, a bolded header, a merged
block spanning several rows — disappears the instant the file is read
into an analysis tool. All that survives the import is the grid of values.
If a color is standing in for some piece of information ("cells shaded
yellow indicate a flagged sample"), that information needs its own column
instead, spelled out as text or a code. The same goes for merged cells: if
a value logically applies to several rows, repeat the value in every row
rather than merging cells to show it once (notice this is exactly what
you did with "Site" and "Observer" above). Extra columns and repeated
values cost you nothing; lost information costs you everything.

### Putting units inside cells

Recording measurements as "5.2 kg" or "12 cm" instead of just "5.2" or
"12" turns a numeric column into a text column the instant your software
reads it — and a text column can't be used in calculations. If every
measurement in a column shares the same unit, put the unit in the column
name instead (`weight_kg`, `distance_cm`). If measurements genuinely come
in mixed units, add a separate column recording the unit for each row
(`weight_unit`) — but the numeric value itself should always be just the
number. This also demonstrates why having appropriate metadata in your repo's
readme file is important ... it can be difficult and sometimes impossible 
to have the units stored in the column name, so it is good practice best for 
your readme file to clearly explain what the units are in the data.

**Try it now:** Fix the "Weight" column so it holds only numbers, with no
unit typed into the cell. Your table should now look like this:

| Frog ID | Age Class | Sex    | Weight  | Site   | Observer |
|---------|-----------|--------|---------|--------|----------|
| 1       | adult     | female | 12.5    | Site A | M. Brown |
| 2       | juvenile  | male   |         | Site A | M. Brown |
| 3       | Adult     | Female | 0       | Site A | M. Brown |

### Using problematic column names

Problematic column names are a lot like the problematic file names from
Chapter 1 — non-descriptive, containing spaces or special characters, or
just human-readable but not computer-readable. Whether you prefer
`weightGrams` or `weight_g`, pick one convention and use it consistently.
Including units directly in the name (`weight_g`, `distance_km`) is a
small habit that saves a lot of confusion, since it means the value itself
never needs a unit typed into it.

**Try it now:** Rename all six column headers to computer-friendly,
`snake_case` names, adding the unit to the weight column's name now that
you know every value is in grams. Your table should now look like this:

| frog_id | age_class | sex    | weight_g | site   | observer |
|---------|-----------|--------|----------|--------|----------|
| 1       | adult     | female | 12.5     | Site A | M. Brown |
| 2       | juvenile  | male   |          | Site A | M. Brown |
| 3       | Adult     | Female | 0        | Site A | M. Brown |

### Applying it: zero vs. missing in the frog data

We already covered the distinction between a true zero and a missing
value earlier in this chapter. Keep it in mind as you work through this
checkpoint — it applies directly to frog 3's weight measurement.

**Try it now:** Checking the field notebook for this survey, you find a
note: *"Frog 3 escaped the net before it could be weighed — recorded 0
by mistake."* Frog 2's blank weight, on the other hand, really is a
correctly-recorded missing value (the scale's battery died partway
through the survey). Fix `weight_g` for frog 3 so it no longer conflates
"escaped, never weighed" with an actual zero-gram measurement:

| frog_id | age_class | sex    | weight_g | site   | observer |
|---------|-----------|--------|----------|--------|----------|
| 1       | adult     | female | 12.5     | Site A | M. Brown |
| 2       | juvenile  | male   |          | Site A | M. Brown |
| 3       | Adult     | Female |          | Site A | M. Brown |

### Same category, different spellings

Inconsistent spelling or capitalization of the same category value is
easy to introduce without noticing — entering "F," "Female," and "f"
interchangeably in a sex column, for instance. Nothing about this breaks
on entry, but it silently undercounts your categories later: filtering
for "female" will miss every row entered as "Female." Deciding on one
spelling per category before you start entering data (and sticking to it)
avoids having to clean this up by hand afterward.

**Try it now:** Standardize the capitalization in `age_class` and `sex`
so the same category is always spelled identically — for this table,
convert everything to lowercase. This is the final fix, so your frog
table is now fully tidy:

| frog_id | age_class | sex    | weight_g | site   | observer |
|---------|-----------|--------|----------|--------|----------|
| 1       | adult     | female | 12.5     | Site A | M. Brown |
| 2       | juvenile  | male   |          | Site A | M. Brown |
| 3       | adult     | female |          | Site A | M. Brown |

## Long vs. wide data

So far, every version of the frog table has had one row per frog and one
column per variable — but there's another common way to lay out the same
kind of data, and it's worth knowing the difference before you run into
it.

Imagine you weighed the same three frogs on three separate site visits.
One natural way to record that is to add a new column for each visit:

| frog_id | weight_visit1 | weight_visit2 | weight_visit3 |
|---------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
| 1       | 11.8           | 12.5           | 13.1           |
| 2       | 9.4            | 10.0           |                |
| 3       | 14.2           | 14.6           | 15.0           |

This is called **wide** data — each visit gets its own column, so the
table grows wider as you collect more observations over time. It's a
format people often reach for instinctively, since it's compact and easy
to scan by eye.

The same information can also be recorded like this, with one row per
frog *per visit*:

| frog_id | visit | weight |
|---------|-------|--------|
| 1       | 1     | 11.8   |
| 1       | 2     | 12.5   |
| 1       | 3     | 13.1   |
| 2       | 1     | 9.4    |
| 2       | 2     | 10.0   |
| 3       | 1     | 14.2   |
| 3       | 2     | 14.6   |
| 3       | 3     | 15.0   |

This is **long** data — each observation (one frog, on one visit) gets
its own row, and "visit" becomes its own variable instead of being spread
across column headers.

Only one of these is tidy. In the wide version, `weight` is really one
variable, but it's split across three separate columns
(`weight_visit1`, `weight_visit2`, `weight_visit3`) — which means the
column headers themselves (`visit1`, `visit2`, `visit3`) are actually
*values* of a variable, not variable names. That's exactly the kind of
problem this chapter has been warning about throughout: a computer
reading this table has no way to know that those three columns all
represent the same underlying variable, weight. The long version doesn't
have this problem — `weight` is one column, `visit` is one column, and
each row is a single, unambiguous observation.

Which format is "better" isn't about file size — despite what you might
expect, long format doesn't reliably take up less space than wide format.
Wide format stores each frog's ID once and spreads its measurements
across columns; long format has to repeat that ID on every row instead.
Long format only tends to win on size when the data is uneven — if frog 2
were only measured twice instead of three times, wide format would still
need a `weight_visit3` column for it, filled in with a blank, while long
format simply wouldn't have that row at all.

The real case for long/tidy format is about what you can *do* with the
data, not how much space it takes up:

- **Vectorized operations work directly.** Filtering, grouping, or
  summarizing by `weight` only works cleanly when `weight` lives in one
  column — not split across `weight_visit1`, `weight_visit2`, and
  `weight_visit3`.
- **The structure doesn't change as you collect more data.** A 4th site
  visit just means more rows. In wide format, it means adding a new
  column to the table itself, which can break code or tools that weren't
  expecting the table to grow sideways.
- **It handles uneven measurement counts naturally.** No need to pad
  missing visits with blank cells.
- **It's what tools like ggplot2 expect.** Mapping a variable to an axis,
  color, or facet requires that variable to already be a single column.
- **It's easier to join with other tables**, since long-format tables
  share key columns cleanly.

Wide format still has its place — it's often exactly the layout you'd
want for a summary table in a report or presentation, where a human is
doing the reading, and a handful of specific tools (correlation matrices,
some repeated-measures formulas) expect wide input directly. But for data
entry, storage, and analysis, long format is almost always the better
default. Later in the course (Chapter 13), you'll learn the
`pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()` functions from the tidyverse, which
convert a dataset between these two formats in a single line of code —
so if you ever do need the wide layout for a table or plot, you're never
stuck re-entering your data by hand to get it.

**Try it now:** Look back at the wide table above. Frog 2 has a blank
cell under `weight_visit3`. Does that blank mean the same thing here as
it did earlier in the chapter — a measurement that's genuinely missing —
or could it mean something else in this context (hint: think about what
a blank half-way through a season of repeat visits might indicate about
when the frog was actually captured)? There's no single right answer;
the point is to notice that "missing" can mean different things
depending on the structure of your data.

## Document, document, document

Following the practices in this chapter should mean most of your data
processing can happen automatically in code, with no manual spreadsheet
editing required. But if you ever do need to make a manual correction —
fixing a typo, standardizing a category — treat it the same way you treat
raw data more generally (Chapter 1): never edit the raw file directly.
Save your correction as a new file, and write down exactly what you
changed and why in your project's README, so that the path from raw data
to analysis-ready data is fully traceable later.

## In-Class Activity: Tracing a Real Case Study Through Tidy Data

For this activity, you won't write any code — instead, you'll work through
a real published case study by hand, tracking how a dataset changes shape
at each step of an analysis, and checking whether it stays tidy along the
way. This case study comes from Hadley Wickham's 2014 paper "Tidy Data,"
which we'll return to again once you've learned R and the tidyverse later
in the course — for now, the goal is just to get comfortable reasoning
about variables, observations, and tidiness across a multi-step analysis.

### The dataset

The case study uses individual-level mortality records from Mexico:
539,530 deaths recorded in 2008, with 55 variables per death, including
the date, time, and cause. A small sample of five of those variables looks
like this:

| yod  | mod | dod | hod | cod |
|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| 2008 | 1   | 1   | 1   | B20 |
| 2008 | 1   | 2   | 4   | I67 |
| 2008 | 1   | 3   | 8   | I50 |
| 2008 | 1   | 4   | 12  | I50 |
| 2008 | 1   | 5   | 16  | K70 |
| 2008 | 1   | 6   | 18  | I21 |
| 2008 | 1   | 7   | 20  | I21 |
| 2008 | 1   | 8   |     | K74 |

(`yod`/`mod`/`dod` = year/month/day of death, `hod` = hour of death, `cod`
= cause of death, coded using a standard disease classification system.)

**Question 1:** What does one row represent here — what's the observation?
What are the variables? Using what you learned earlier in this chapter,
is this table tidy? Why or why not?

### The goal

The researcher's question is: *do some causes of death have an unusual
pattern of what time of day they happen, compared to deaths in general?*
For instance, maybe traffic accidents cluster around commute hours, while
heart attacks don't follow any particular hourly pattern at all.

### Step 1: Counting deaths by hour and cause

The first step collapses the 539,530 individual death records down into
one row per hour-of-day/cause-of-day combination, counting how many
deaths of each cause happened in each hour. A few rows of the result look
like this:

| hod | cod | freq |
|-----|-----|------|
| 8   | B16 | 4    |
| 8   | E84 | 3    |
| 8   | I21 | 2205 |
| 8   | N18 | 315  |
| 9   | B16 | 7    |
| 9   | I21 | 2209 |

**Question 2:** What changed about what a "row" represents, compared to
the original table? Is this new table still tidy? What are its variables?

### Step 2: Joining in disease names

The disease codes (`B16`, `I21`, etc.) aren't meaningful on their own, so
the researcher combines this table with a second lookup table that maps
each code to a readable disease name, matching rows using the shared `cod`
column. The result adds one new column, `disease`:

| hod | cod | freq | disease                     |
|-----|-----|------|------------------------------|
| 8   | B16 | 4    | Acute hepatitis B            |
| 8   | I21 | 2205 | Acute myocardial infarction  |
| 9   | B16 | 7    | Acute hepatitis B            |
| 9   | I21 | 2209 | Acute myocardial infarction  |

**Question 3:** Two separate tables (the hourly counts, and the disease
code lookup) got combined into one, matched on a shared column. Why might
it be better to store the disease code separately from the readable name
in the first place, rather than just writing out the disease name every
time, from the very start of data entry? (Hint: think back to the
"problematic column names" and "consistent spelling" issues from earlier
in this chapter.)

### Step 3: Converting counts to proportions

Some causes of death are far more common than others — about 46,800
deaths from heart attack that year, versus only about 10 from avalanche.
Comparing raw counts across causes this different in scale wouldn't be
meaningful, so the researcher instead computes, for each cause, what
*proportion* of that cause's deaths happened in each hour (each cause's
proportions sum to 1 across all 24 hours):

| hod | cod | freq | disease                     | prop |
|-----|-----|------|------------------------------|------|
| 8   | B16 | 4    | Acute hepatitis B            | 0.04 |
| 8   | I21 | 2205 | Acute myocardial infarction  | 0.05 |
| 9   | B16 | 7    | Acute hepatitis B            | 0.07 |
| 9   | I21 | 2209 | Acute myocardial infarction  | 0.05 |

**Question 4:** This calculation had to be done separately *within* each
disease (each disease's proportions are computed only from that disease's
own hourly counts, not mixed with any other disease's numbers). Why does
having the data in tidy form — one row per hour/cause combination — make
it possible to calculate this "by group" without needing to physically
split the data into separate tables first?

### Step 4: Adding the overall baseline pattern

To tell whether a disease's hourly pattern is unusual, you need something
to compare it to: the overall hourly death rate, across all causes
combined. The researcher computes that separately, then merges it back
into the same table as a new column, `prop_all`, so every row can be
compared directly against the population-wide baseline for that hour:

| hod | cod | freq | disease                     | prop | prop_all |
|-----|-----|------|------------------------------|------|----------|
| 8   | B16 | 4    | Acute hepatitis B            | 0.04 | 0.04     |
| 8   | I21 | 2205 | Acute myocardial infarction  | 0.05 | 0.04     |
| 9   | B16 | 7    | Acute hepatitis B            | 0.07 | 0.04     |
| 9   | I21 | 2209 | Acute myocardial infarction  | 0.05 | 0.04     |

**Question 5:** Notice `prop_all` repeats the same value (0.04) for every
disease within hour 8, and a different repeated value for hour 9. Does
this repetition violate any tidy data principle? Why or why not?

### Step 5: Measuring how "unusual" each disease is

For each disease, the researcher now has two columns to compare: its own
hourly pattern (`prop`) and the overall baseline (`prop_all`). Taking the
average squared difference between these two columns, across all 24
hours, gives a single number per disease measuring how much that disease's
timing deviates from the population-wide pattern. Diseases with very few
total deaths (under 50 for the year) are excluded, since their hourly
patterns are too noisy to say anything meaningful.

**Question 6:** This step collapses 24 rows (one per hour) down to a
single deviation score, one per disease. What table structure would you
expect this result to have — what's a row, and what are the columns?

### Step 6: Flagging the unusual diseases

Plotting each disease's deviation score against its total death count (on
a log-log scale) and fitting a trend line, the researcher flags diseases
whose deviation is much higher than expected for their sample size — a
residual greater than 1.5 above the trend line.

The diseases that stood out fell into three groups, each with a distinct
daily rhythm: homicide deaths clustered in the evening/nighttime hours;
drowning deaths clustered in the afternoon; and transportation-related
deaths clustered around typical commute hours.

**Question 7:** Look back over Steps 1–6. At no point did the data need
to be reshaped into a "wide" format (with separate columns for each hour,
or each disease) to perform any of these calculations — counting,
joining, computing proportions, merging in a baseline, and measuring
deviation. Why do you think keeping the data in this consistent
long/tidy shape throughout made each of these steps easier than it would
have been in some other layout?

### What to submit in Canvas

Submit your written answers to Questions 1–7. There's no single "correct"
phrasing expected — the goal is to demonstrate that you can identify
variables, observations, and tidiness at each stage of a real analysis,
and reason about why the tidy structure was helpful throughout.
